title: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry
hook: a sixteen-year-old in Madurai lies down on the floor and acts out his own death
carry: karma: seva as a life · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana: Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry

segments.voice: Last week closed on three roads: karma with Vivekananda, bhakti with Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, jnana with I am Brahman. Did you apologize first? This week, a new teacher on the jnana road. Day three hundred sixteen.

Madurai, South India, the summer of 1896. A sixteen-year-old boy named Venkataraman is alone in a room in his uncle's house. He's healthy. Nothing is wrong. And suddenly he's hit by an overwhelming fear that he's about to die. Most of us would call someone, or go for a walk, or distract ourselves. He does something else. He lies down on the floor, stretches out his limbs like a corpse, holds his breath, and says to himself: all right. Death has come. What does it mean? What is it that's dying?
screen: `MADURAI, 1896.` → `A SUDDEN FEAR OF DEATH.` → `HE LIES DOWN AND ASKS.`

segments.voice: Lying there, as he later told it, he reasoned it through. This body is dead. They'll carry it to the cremation ground and burn it. But with the body dead, am I dead? Is the body I? And in that moment, he said, he knew directly that he was not the body: that the I, the Self, was something the death of the body couldn't touch. The fear vanished and never came back. A few weeks later he left home, leaving a short note, and took a train toward a sacred mountain called Arunachala, in the town of Tiruvannamalai. He stayed at that mountain for the rest of his life, more than fifty years. People came to call him Ramana Maharshi, and they came from all over the world to sit with him. Often he said nothing at all. When he did teach, the heart of it was a single question: who am I? Not as a riddle to answer with words. Not I'm a teacher, I'm a parent, I'm tired. Those are things you have, he'd say, in effect, not what you are. Instead, turn the question around and follow the feeling of I back to where it comes from. That's self-inquiry, and it's the jnana road with almost nothing extra: no ritual required, no long study, just attention turned toward its source. What he did at sixteen on that floor, he spent fifty years inviting other people to try, gently, from wherever they were.
screen: `THE BODY DIES. AM I DEAD?` · `THE FEAR NEVER CAME BACK.` · `FIFTY YEARS AT ARUNACHALA.` · `ONE QUESTION: WHO AM I?` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask the question once, quietly: who am I? Don't answer with a name or a role. Just notice the plain sense of being here, this I that's listening. When a thought comes, ask gently: to whom did this thought come? To me. And who am I? Then rest in the space where the answer would be. It's fine if nothing happens. The looking is the practice. If you pray, you can rest in God as the source of that I. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action was to lie down and look, and he spent his life inviting others to turn and look too.

Your line names this final week's three roads: karma, seva as a life; bhakti, the Gita Govinda; jnana, Ramana Maharshi's self-inquiry. Today, when you say I, pause once, and ask who. Day three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Visitors to Ramana Maharshi's ashram at Tiruvannamalai sit in silence in his old hall and walk around the hill of Arunachala; followers practice self-inquiry by turning attention to the sense of I rather than to its thoughts.

original.note: Tamil: 'who am I?', the title of Ramana Maharshi's short teaching text on self-inquiry.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'who am I?' is a question about personality.
what it means: turn attention back toward the sense of I and rest in its source, beneath every role.
what a scholar hears: atma-vichara, self-inquiry. Ramana's Tamil text Nan Yar? began as answers to a visitor's questions around 1901; his teaching is usually read in an Advaita frame.

sources.ref: Ramana Maharshi's account of his death experience (1896), as recorded by his followers

notes: Ramana Maharshi (1879–1950): death experience in Madurai, July 1896, at sixteen; arrived at Tiruvannamalai 1 September 1896; stayed until his death in 1950. Confirm.
The death experience is paraphrased from his own later account; no English translation is quoted (they are 20th-century).
Nan Yar? origin (answers to Sivaprakasam Pillai, c. 1901–02); confirm.
The original-language item is Tamil, not Sanskrit, because Ramana taught in Tamil; the guide asks for Devanagari for Hindu words. Confirm acceptable, or use कोऽहम् (ko'ham).
